title: Number of Matching Subsequences
description: Brute force to optimized: rescanning s per word versus bucketing words by their next needed character.

blocks.text: Given a string s and an array of strings words, count how many words in the array are subsequences of s.

blocks.caption: Bucket every word by the character it is waiting for; advance them all in one shared pass over s

blocks.title: Analogy: Checking Many Shopping Lists Against One Long Aisle at Once
blocks.text: Like walking down one long store aisle a single time while simultaneously checking off items from many different shopping lists at once, rather than walking the entire aisle separately for every single list.

blocks.caption: Count how many words can be found, in order, as subsequences of s

blocks.text: The single word matches s exactly, so it counts as a valid subsequence, giving 1.

Before checking each word against s independently, notice that every one of those checks scans the same string s, and doing that scan once per word throws away an obvious opportunity: many words could be advanced together during a single shared pass.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: The standard two-pointer subsequence check for one word only ever cares about one thing at any moment: what is the very next character this word still needs to find?

Observation 2: If many words are being checked at once, at any given point in s, several of them might all be waiting for the same next character, meaning a single character of s can potentially advance multiple words simultaneously, not just one.

Observation 3: Grouping words by "the character they are currently waiting for", using a hash map from character to a list of waiting words each tracked by its current position, makes this simultaneous advancement mechanical: whenever that character is reached in s, every word currently in its bucket gets to advance by one position at once.

Observation 4: After a word advances, it either becomes fully matched, if it just consumed its last character, or moves into a different bucket, for whichever character it needs next, ready to be advanced again whenever that character is later reached in s.

Whenever many independent linear scans need to run over the exact same sequence, look for a way to flip the loop order: scan the shared sequence once, and let each item currently "waiting" on the current position advance together, instead of repeating the shared scan once per item.
This turns "scan s once per word" into "scan s exactly once, total", with every word's own progress tracked lazily through hash map buckets instead of through its own dedicated pass.
For every word independently, check whether it is a subsequence of s using the standard two pointer scan, rescanning s from the beginning for every single word.

items: For every word, use two pointers to check whether it appears in s in order.
Count how many words pass this check.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: is_subsequence scans every character of s unconditionally, even after the word has already been fully matched, since stopping early would need an extra check that saves little for typically short words.
The bounds check before comparing prevents an out-of-bounds access into word once its pointer has already reached the end.
The final check confirms every character of word was matched in order, not just some prefix of it, since reaching the end of s without the pointer catching up means the word was never fully found.

blocks.text: Every word is correctly checked as a subsequence of s using the standard two pointer scan, so the count is correct.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(number of words times length of s), rescanning s completely for every word.
Space: O(1) extra, not counting the words themselves.
Limitation: rescanning s from scratch for every word wastes the opportunity to advance many words together during a single pass over s.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force's waste is structural: it repeats the exact same walk through s, once per word, even though most of that walk is identical work between different words, just checking against the same characters over and over. The fix does not speed up any single word's check, a subsequence check is already inherently linear, it instead shares the single walk through s across every word simultaneously. Grouping words by the one piece of information that actually matters at any moment, which character each is currently waiting for, turns the walk through s into a dispatch mechanism: at each character of s, every word waiting for exactly that character gets advanced together, for free, as a side effect of the single shared scan, rather than needing its own dedicated scan.

Group every word by the very next character it still needs to match, using a hash map from character to a list of (word, position) pairs currently waiting on that character. Scan s exactly once, character by character. At each character of s, take every word currently waiting for that exact character, advance its position by one, and either move it into the bucket for whatever character it needs next, or count it as fully matched if its position has reached the end of the word. This lets a single pass over s advance every word simultaneously, instead of one word at a time.
Bucket words by the next character each one is waiting for, and advance every waiting word together as s is scanned once.

blocks.caption: Optimized: bucket words by their next needed character, advance them all in one pass over s

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(length of s plus total characters across all words), since every character of every word is examined at most once overall.
Space: O(total characters across all words), for the waiting buckets.

Every word is, at any given moment, waiting for exactly one specific character, the next one it still needs; placing it into the bucket for that character means it will automatically be found and advanced the next time that character is encountered while scanning s, with no separate lookup or search needed. Since s is scanned exactly once from start to end, and every word's position only ever moves forward, each word is guaranteed to be advanced through every one of its own characters in the correct order, exactly reproducing what an individual two-pointer scan would have done, just interleaved with every other word's progress instead of run separately.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Bucket key","Meaning"],"rows":[["A character c","Every word currently waiting for its next character to be c"],["A word reaching its own final position","Fully matched; counted and removed from further consideration"]]}

items: Every word starts in the bucket for its own first character, since before any of s has been scanned, that first character is what every word is waiting for.
The current character's bucket is read and immediately cleared before processing its contents, so its stored list can be safely reused for whatever new words are later routed there.
Advancing a word's position by 1 and checking whether it now equals the word's length distinguishes "fully matched" from "needs to move to a new bucket" in a single comparison.
A word that has not yet finished is re-inserted into the bucket for its new next character, ready to be picked up again whenever that character is later encountered in s.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Approach","Time","Space","Notes"],"rows":[["Brute force (rescan s per word)","O(words times length of s)","O(1) extra","Every word independently rescans the entirety of s from the beginning"],["Optimized (bucket by next needed character)","O(length of s plus total word characters)","O(total word characters)","s is scanned exactly once; every character of every word is examined at most once overall, across the whole run"]]}

blocks.text: The key insight is inverting the usual "for each word, scan s" loop order into "scan s once, advance all waiting words together", a pattern useful whenever many independent linear scans over the same sequence can be merged into a single shared pass.

items: Clearing a character's waiting bucket before finishing processing its current contents in a way that loses entries, when a word can never re-enter the very bucket it was just read from in the same step, since its next needed character always differs from the one just matched.

Forgetting to handle duplicate words in the input, though the bucket approach naturally handles them correctly since each occurrence is tracked as its own independent waiting entry, not deduplicated by value.
Advancing a word's position without checking whether it has reached the word's full length, which would silently continue tracking an already-fully-matched word as if it still needed more characters.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Edge case","Expected behavior"],"rows":[["A word longer than s","Can never be fully matched and simply never gets counted, since it will always still be waiting for some character once s is exhausted"],["An empty words array","Trivially returns a count of 0, since there is nothing to bucket or advance at all"]]}

items: Describe the bucket approach as "flipping the loop order": instead of iterating words in the outer loop and s in the inner loop, s becomes the outer loop and the currently relevant words become the inner one, which is the single sentence that captures the whole optimization.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Check many words or patterns against the same shared sequence" points toward flipping the loop order: scan the shared sequence once, and advance every currently-relevant item together, instead of rescanning per item.

items: How would you handle this if s were extremely long and arrived as a live stream, one character at a time? The bucket-based approach adapts directly, since it already processes s character by character; just feed streamed characters in as they arrive instead of iterating a stored string.

What if words could be added or removed dynamically between queries on the same s? Newly added words would need their own bucket entry inserted at their first character; removed words would need to be found and removed from whichever bucket they currently occupy, requiring a way to locate a word's current bucket directly.

How would you extend this to count the longest word that is a subsequence, rather than just how many words qualify? Track each word's own length alongside its progress, and update a running maximum whenever a word becomes fully matched, instead of just incrementing a count.
Same "flip the loop order to share one pass across many items" insight as event-driven simulation techniques and any "many watchers on one shared timeline" style problem.
Same "bucket by the next required key" philosophy as Word Pattern's bijection maps, though applied here to positions within words rather than to whole values.
Same underlying two-pointer subsequence check as Is Subsequence, just run for many words simultaneously instead of one at a time.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(words times length of s) time, O(1) extra space.
Optimized (bucket by next needed character): O(length of s plus total word characters) time, O(total word characters) space.

items: Pattern: Bucket words by their next needed character, advancing all waiting words together during a single scan of s
Core Idea: Instead of rescanning s once per word, scan s exactly once and let every word waiting for the current character advance simultaneously, tracked via hash map buckets
Time: O(length of s plus total word characters)
Space: O(total word characters), for the waiting buckets
Most Important Observation: Many independent linear scans over the same sequence can often be merged into a single shared pass by grouping items by what they are each currently waiting for
Interview Difficulty: Hard
One-line memory trick: Flip the loop: scan s once, let waiting words hop forward together
